title: Prefetch Fidelity Gates: SDK Playbook for Latency-Budgeted Tooling and Structured Output
content:
Purpose
This is a working PRD/playbook proposing a lightweight "fidelity gate" model for SDK-driven prefetching and tool calling inside Hosted API streaming flows. The intent is to give application developers a simple surface to declaratively express latency budgets and desired output fidelity, while the SDK and server runtime make predictable tradeoffs (prefetch intensity, structured output enforcement, speculative toolcalls) to hit latency SLOs.

Background / problem statement
- Customers building interactive experiences demand predictable tail latency even when invoking external tools or requiring high-quality structured outputs.
- Current choices are binary: always prefetch everything (too expensive/slow) or lazy call tools (higher tail-latency and jitter).
- Streaming flows add complexity: partial tokens vs final structured frames require coordinated behavior between SDK and server to avoid confusing clients.

Goals
- Provide a small, composable SDK surface so app teams can specify per-call latency budget and fidelity preference.
- Let runtime choose prefetch profiles and speculative tool strategies to maximize successful high-fidelity responses under budget.
- Maintain strong observability: see which fidelity gates were applied, prefetch hit/miss, speculative vs sync tool outcomes, and QoR metrics on structured output.

Non-goals
- This doc does not attempt to replace full rollout/AB pipelines for model or quantization swaps.
- Not prescribing server-side kernel selection internals; focus is on the API/SDK and control signals.

High-level design
- Fidelity gates: a small enum that travels with each request: NONE | CONSERVATIVE | BALANCED | AGGRESSIVE. Each gate maps to a server-side prefetch profile and a speculative-tool policy.
- Latency budget: clients can pass target p50/p95 budget (ms) or a single latency_slo_ms value. Server and SDK weight decisions against this budget.
- Streaming semantics: incremental text tokens are emitted as usual, but the server tags frames with fidelity metadata and checkpoint markers. Structured output (final JSON payloads) can be sent as a final 'commit frame' when ready or as progressive partial structured checkpoints.

Example SDK surface (sketch)
- call generation with fidelity options:
  const resp = await Redwood.hosted.generate({
    model: 'rw-instruct-v2',
    prompt,
    streaming: true,
    fidelity_gate: 'BALANCED',
    latency_slo_ms: 400,
    structured_schema: 'invoice-v1' // optional identifier
  })
- SDK will expose on('frame', cb) events with: {type: 'token'|'partial_struct'|'commit', fidelity_gate_applied, trace_id}
- Callback hooks: on('prefetch_decision', info) and on('tool_call_outcome', info) for client telemetry.

Prefetch profiles (server mapping)
- NONE: no prefetch; lazy tool invocation only.
- CONSERVATIVE: small prefix cache warm; pre-resolve light-weight tools (caching strong matches), no heavy speculative calls.
- BALANCED: richer prefix warm, speculatively call fast tools with cached fallbacks, schedule heavy tool calls only if remaining budget allows.
- AGGRESSIVE: call candidate tools speculatively early and merge results into streaming responses; higher cost but increases chance of high-fidelity final structured commit.

Tool calling model
- Tools divided into tiers: FAST_READ (cacheable, low-latency), WORKER (medium latency), HEAVY_JOB (long-running).
- Speculative vs sync: under AGGRESSIVE/BALANCED the runtime may speculative-invoke FAST_READ and WORKER tasks and attach a tool_token in streaming frames enabling client-side optimistic UI. If the speculative result fails or returns low confidence, runtime falls back to a cheaper output and logs event.
- Tool idempotency and replay: SDK will attach a request id to tool calls and accept idempotent replays for retry/fallback.

Structured output handling
- Schema-driven commit frame: final structured outputs are validated against the provided structured_schema. If validation fails, runtime emits a 'schema-error' partial structured frame and a less structured fallback content.
- Progressive structured checkpoints: server can emit checkpoint frames with confidence scores so client can progressively render validated sections (e.g., header validated, line-items pending).

SDK ergonomics & UX principles
- Minimal surface: default to BALANCED if unspecified. Provide opinionated defaults so teams rarely need to tune.
- Observability-first: expose small, typed events to the app so product telemetry ties fidelity decisions to UX metrics.
- Explicit fallbacks: easy hooks for apps to register fallback renderers for partial/failed structured commits.
- Backpressure friendly: SDK exposes a lightweight 'latency_pressure' signal when budgets are tight so UI can reduce rendering fidelity (reduce polling frequency, show skeletons).

Telemetry & trace model
- Every request must include trace_id and fidelity_gate_applied in root telemetry.
- Sampled fields: prefetch_profile, speculative_tool_calls (list of tiers called), tool_outcomes (success|fail|timeout), final_struct_confidence, total_server_latency_ms, tokenized_tail_ms.
- Dashboards: per-route fidelity success rate, cost delta vs NONE, and structured-schema regression alerting (schema validation failures over time).

Backward compatibility and migration path
- Default behavior remains unchanged when fidelity fields are omitted.
- Provide server-side feature flag to enable fidelity gates per-customer so we can gate rollout.
- SDK will include a compatibility layer that maps legacy prefetch flags to fidelity_gate values.

Security and privacy notes
- Speculative tool results must respect data residency and PII rules. The runtime should not speculatively send sensitive documents to external tools unless the customer has tool-federation consent enabled.
- Audit logs must record speculative tool invocations and whether the speculative output contributed to a final commit.

Operational concerns and cost model
- AGGRESSIVE gates increase compute and tool call rates; surface an estimated cost increase metric in telemetry to educate customers.
- Add circuit-breakers for repeated speculative failures to avoid runaway tool costs.

Rollout plan / experiments
1) Internal lab: A/B experiment with 3 internal teams using BALANCED default vs NONE to measure p95 latency and final fidelity for 2 weeks. Metric: p95 tail latency reduction vs structured-output acceptance rate.
2) Opt-in alpha: expose fidelity gate flag to a small set of beta customers behind a feature flag. Collect telemetry and cost impact.
3) Canary: enable BALANCED by default for low-traffic routes with automatic fallback to NONE on cost threshold.
4) Gradual global rollout once metrics meet target: p95 latency < baseline + 10% and structured commit acceptance > 90%.

Open questions / design tradeoffs
- Should structured_schema be a declarative JSON schema blob or a schema id that maps to server-validated definitions? (prefer schema id for size and management).
- How to rank tools to decide speculative candidates? (hybrid of historical success rate and cost).
- UX for client when speculative content appears then is retracted—best practices and developer guidance required.

Next steps (immediate owners)
- Product: finalize experiment success criteria (Priya)
- Applied ML / Runtime: define server prefetch mapping and speculative tool gating knobs (Daniel, Omar)
- SDK: prototype event hooks and surface above (Maya)
- Observability: add fidelity telemetry signals and dashboards (Leah)

Appendix: quick checklist for SDK implementers
- [ ] Accept fidelity_gate and latency_slo_ms in request payload
- [ ] Emit 'prefetch_decision' and 'tool_call_outcome' events to client callbacks
- [ ] Tag every streaming frame with fidelity metadata and trace_id
- [ ] Support structured_schema identifier and gracefully handle 'schema-error' frames
- [ ] Sample telemetry at 1% by default; configurable per-customer

This is a living draft — feedback welcome, especially from SDK, runtime and solutions teams on where the tradeoffs should sit between cost and fidelity.
